overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Limits of the Double Portion
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 52a–52b
overview.hebrewSource: הַבְּכוֹר נוֹטֵל פִּי שְׁנַיִם בְּנִכְסֵי הָאָב, וְאֵינוֹ נוֹטֵל פִּי שְׁנַיִם בְּנִכְסֵי הָאֵם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: This daf completes the mishna on the firstborn's double portion: he takes it only from the father's property, never the mother's, never from value that appreciated after death, and never from property still due to the father but not yet in his possession. The Gemara grounds each limit in the verse 'all that he has' (Deut. 21:17) and extends the same restrictions to a wife's marriage contract, daughters' sustenance, and a yavam's levirate inheritance. A new mishna then asks which acquisitions — the firstborn's extra portion, a husband's inheritance of his wife, a yavam's levirate share, and gifts — must revert to their original owners in the Jubilee Year, generating a four-way tannaitic dispute. The daf, and the whole first perek of Bekhorot, ends with the practicalities of a husband inheriting his late wife's family burial plot.

slides.title: 👑 Four Things the Firstborn Does NOT Get Double
slides.subtitle: All four grounded in the same phrase: 'all that he has'
rows: 'The law of primogeniture is his' — the law applies to a man's heirs, not a woman's
'A double portion of ALL THAT HE HAS' — the increase wasn't his at death
Property due the father but not possessed
Same phrase — property not yet in hand doesn't count as 'what he has'
Automatic increase (e.g., unripe grain becoming ripe)
Included by repetition of the mishna's language, even without labor

slides.title: 📈 The Same Rule, Three More Contexts
slides.subtitle: Wife, daughters, and yavam all face the identical limitation

boxes.title: Wife's Ketubah
items: Cannot claim increase in value, though a creditor normally could (Shmuel)
Rabbi Abba: this is one of the leniencies the Sages built into a marriage contract

boxes.title: Daughters' Sustenance
items: A stipulation in the ketubah is treated like the ketubah itself
Cannot claim what the ketubah itself cannot claim

boxes.title: The Yavam
items: Abaye: excluded only for increase between death and levirate marriage — after that, he does take it, since he has 'succeeded' his brother

callout.label: Rava's stricter view:
callout.text: Even the increase between levirate marriage and the actual distribution is excluded — a yavam, like a firstborn, has no special claim before the inheritance is formally divided.

slides.title: 🔄 Which Portions Return in the Jubilee Year?
slides.subtitle: The new mishna's four-way dispute

nodes.content: ❓ Fields acquired by sale return to original owners in the Jubilee Year — but what about the firstborn's extra share, a husband's inheritance, a yavam's share, and gifts?
🟢 Rabbi Meir: none of them return — each is an inheritance or gift, not a sale, and 'sold' land alone must return

columns.label: Rabbis
columns.content: A gift IS like a sale ('you shall return' teaches this) — so gifts return, but true inheritances (firstborn, husband, yavam) do not

columns.label: R' Elazar
columns.content: ALL of these — including the firstborn's portion — count as gifts and DO return

nodes.content: 👨‍👩‍👧 Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka: even a husband's inheritance from his wife must return to her family, deducting its monetary value

callout.label: Rav Sheshet's clarification:
callout.text: 'Do not return' in the mishna means the firstborn doesn't lose his portion for nothing — when the property IS redistributed, he again takes his double share.

slides.title: ⚖️ Are Divided Brothers 'Purchasers' From Each Other?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling and Rabbi Elazar's objection

lines.speaker: R' Yochanan
lines.text: Brothers who divide an inherited estate are considered purchasers from one another — so they must return their shares to each other in the Jubilee Year.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But the mishna explicitly lists the firstborn's portion among those that do NOT return in the Jubilee!

lines.speaker: R' Elazar
lines.text: 'Do not return' means they don't return for nothing — the firstborn gets his double share again once redistribution happens.

lines.speaker: Confirmed
lines.text: Ravin cites R' Yoḥanan (or R' Elazar ben Shammua): yes — 'they return' really does mean forfeiting the portion entirely, for naught.

slides.title: 🪦 Deducting the Cost of a Family Burial Plot
slides.label: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka's ruling explained:
slides.text: A husband who inherits his wife's property must sometimes return it to her family — for example, if she bequeathed him the family graveyard. Since burying outsiders' relatives there would be a family disgrace, the Sages ruled he must return the plot itself, but first deduct from its value the cost of his wife's own burial there, since a husband is obligated to bury his wife. This closes the first perek of Bekhorot, 'Yesh Bekhor.'

summary.principle: The firstborn's double portion, like a wife's ketubah claim, daughters' sustenance, and a yavam's share, is strictly limited to the father's actual possessions at death — never appreciation, never property merely due — and the same 'gift vs. inheritance' distinction determines what returns in the Jubilee Year.

flowSteps.content: 👑 The firstborn's double portion comes only from what the father actually possessed at death
📈 The same limit extends to wife's ketubah, daughters' sustenance, and the yavam's levirate share

columns.content: 🔄 Jubilee dispute: R' Meir says none return; Rabbis say gifts do, inheritances don't; R' Elazar says all return
🪦 A husband inheriting a family graveyard must return it, minus his wife's burial costs

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'All that he has' (Deut. 21:17) fixes the boundary of every double-portion and inheritance-based claim

quiz.q: From which parent's property does a firstborn son take a double portion?
o: Both parents equally
Only the mother's property
Only the father's property
Neither — firstborns get no special share
quiz.e: The mishna states that the firstborn takes a double portion only from his father's property, deriving from 'the law of primogeniture is his' (Deuteronomy 21:17) that this law applies to a man, not a woman.

quiz.q: Why can't the firstborn claim double the increase in the value of property that appreciated after his father's death?
o: Because appreciation is never inherited by anyone
Because the verse specifies 'all that he HAS' — the appreciation was not in the father's possession at death
Because only real estate can appreciate
Because the firstborn forfeits all rights after the father's death
quiz.e: The Gemara derives this from the phrase 'all that he has' (Deuteronomy 21:17): since the enhanced value did not exist in the father's possession at the time of his death, it falls outside the double portion.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir, why don't the firstborn's extra portion, a husband's inheritance from his wife, and a yavam's levirate share need to return to original owners in the Jubilee Year?
o: Because they are all considered sales
Because they are all considered inheritances (or in the firstborn's case, a Torah-called 'gift' treated like inheritance), not sales, and only sold land returns
Because the Jubilee Year law doesn't apply to any of them
Because they were never legally acquired
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir holds that only land acquired through sale must return in the Jubilee Year; these cases are each rooted in inheritance (or gift-like inheritance), which the Torah does not require to be returned.

quiz.q: What does Rabbi Elazar (as clarified by Ravin's report) mean by saying the firstborn's portion 'returns' in the Jubilee Year?
o: The firstborn simply gets an equal share alongside his brothers again next cycle
The firstborn forfeits the extra portion entirely, for naught, when the Jubilee arrives
The land physically changes location
Nothing changes at all
quiz.e: Rav Ḥama cites the tradition that Rabbi Elazar's position means the firstborn's double portion 'returns for naught' — he genuinely loses that extra share when the Jubilee Year comes, according to this opinion.

quiz.q: Why must a husband who inherited his wife's family graveyard deduct part of its monetary value when returning it to her family, according to the baraita cited?
o: Because he must pay a fine for delaying the return
Because he should deduct the cost of his wife's own burial there, since a husband is obligated to pay for his wife's burial
Because graveyards are always worth less than their sale price
Because the family owes him for maintenance costs
quiz.e: The baraita explains that since a husband bears the financial obligation to bury his wife, when he returns the family plot he first deducts the value of his wife's grave from what he owes.
